title: Presentation Skills
subtitle: General topic guide: audience, technical storytelling, evidence, visual communication, demos, timing, and questions.
contentMarkdown:
## Scope

**General study guide — no L31 lecture slides were supplied.** This guide focuses on explaining and defending a software engineering project. Suggested timings are practice examples, not an official presentation rubric. Check any course-specific instructions separately.

## 1. Start with the audience and outcome

A presentation is successful when the audience can understand the relevant problem, assess the evidence and act on the conclusion. Start by writing one sentence describing what they should know, believe or decide by the end.

Identify their background and concerns. A client may care about a completed workflow and its benefit; an engineering examiner may ask how the design meets requirements and what evidence supports quality claims. A mixed audience needs a plain-language overview before technical depth. Define specialised terms at first use and avoid assuming everyone knows your project vocabulary.

## 2. Build a reasoned narrative

A useful structure is **problem → constraints → approach → evidence → limitations → next step**. State the user problem before showing implementation details. Explain a design choice through the requirement it addresses, alternatives considered and the resulting trade-off.

Weak: “We used a queue because it is modern.” Stronger: “Payment processing may pause; a durable queue lets us accept pending orders while workers recover. We must now handle duplicates and communicate pending status.” The second explanation connects the mechanism to a need and acknowledges its cost.

| Part | Audience question |
|---|---|
| Problem | Who is affected and why does it matter? |
| Requirements | What must the solution achieve? |
| Approach | Why was this design chosen? |
| Demonstration | Can we see the important workflow? |
| Evidence | What supports the claimed behaviour and quality? |
| Limitations | What remains incomplete or uncertain? |
| Next step | What decision or action follows? |

## 3. Claims need appropriate evidence

A screenshot can show that a screen exists; it does not prove its server-side permissions. A unit-test count does not establish production capacity. Match each claim to an observation that can support it.

For a performance claim, report the workload, environment, sample or duration, metric and result. “p95 response time was 240 ms during a ten-minute run at 100 requests/second on the stated test environment” is assessable. “The system is very fast” is not. Do not extrapolate a small test to every production condition.

Distinguish **implemented**, **tested**, **demonstrated**, **planned** and **assumed**. If presenting sample data or a recorded demo, label it. Attribute external diagrams, code and results so original work and borrowed material are clear.

## 4. Make visuals carry one clear message

Use readable text, sufficient contrast and direct labels. A slide title can state its conclusion, such as “Two app replicas still share one database failure point.” Include only the detail needed for that conclusion.

Use a diagram for structure or flows, a chart for a measured comparison, and a short table for trade-offs. Explain arrow direction and notation; do not present a whole unreadable architecture poster. Highlight the part currently being discussed.

Avoid colour as the only signal: combine it with text, symbols or line styles. Include units, axes and baselines in charts. A truncated axis can exaggerate differences; if necessary for a particular analysis, make the scale explicit and explain it. Cite the source of external data.

For code, show a small relevant excerpt and explain its purpose or invariant. Reading an entire source file aloud rarely helps the audience understand the design.

## 5. A demo is a planned experiment

Choose a user journey that demonstrates a central requirement. State the starting condition, action and expected outcome. Prepare realistic, non-sensitive sample data and reset the application to a known state before rehearsal and delivery.

Include one useful negative case when time permits, such as a rejected unauthorised request. Explain what it proves and what it does not. Keep credentials and personal data out of projected screens and logs.

Prepare a fallback: a clearly labelled recording, screenshots or a walkthrough of expected results. If the live demo fails, acknowledge the failure, attempt a bounded recovery and switch to the fallback. Do not spend all remaining time debugging or represent recorded output as live evidence.

## 6. Timing and rehearsal

An illustrative ten-minute plan is one minute for the problem, one for requirements, two for design, three for the demo, two for evidence and limitations, and one for the conclusion. Adapt to the actual rubric and whether questions are included in the allocation.

Rehearse aloud with the real slides, device and demo state. Measure transitions and setup time as well as speaking time. Identify optional detail to cut if running late; protect the core conclusion and evidence. Appendix slides can hold deeper diagrams and results for questions.

A useful rehearsal review asks: Where did the listener lose the thread? Which claim lacked evidence? Which term needed explanation? Improve those specific issues rather than only repeating the same script.

## 7. Delivery and team coordination

Speak at a pace that leaves time to interpret diagrams. Use pauses at transitions and signpost connections: “This requirement explains the next design choice.” Face the audience, keep pointing purposeful and avoid reading slide paragraphs verbatim.

Assign clear speaking roles and handoffs in team presentations. Everyone should understand the overall system even when specialising in one section. Rehearse the laptop or slide-control handoff. Avoid inconsistent terminology and repeated introductions that consume the available time.

## 8. Questions and honest uncertainty

Listen to the whole question, clarify ambiguity if needed, answer the central point first, then provide evidence. If a premise is incorrect, explain the relevant distinction respectfully. Stay within what you can substantiate.

If you do not know, say what is known and how you would verify the missing part. “We measured single-zone failure recovery; we have not tested a regional outage” is more useful than inventing a number. Record follow-up commitments only when you can fulfil them.

## 9. Worked example: defend a queue

**Claim:** orders can remain pending during a temporary payment-worker outage. **Design:** durable queue plus workers. **Demo:** stop a worker, submit an order, show pending state, restart and observe completion. **Evidence:** queue depth, processing logs and one recorded payment effect per order ID. **Limitation:** the result depends on queue capacity, retention and correct duplicate handling. **Next step:** test longer outages and capacity limits.

This connects requirement, mechanism and evidence without claiming that one demonstration proves every reliability property.
tldr: Start with **audience, purpose and a clear intended outcome**.
Match claims to evidence; distinguish **implemented, tested and planned**.
Use readable, labelled visuals and explain diagram conventions.
Rehearse the complete demo and prepare an **honestly labelled fallback**.
Answer questions directly; state uncertainty instead of inventing results.

mcqs.q: What is the strongest starting point for planning a presentation?
mcqs.explanation: Audience and purpose determine which content and level of detail are useful.

mcqs.q: Which design explanation is strongest?
options: Connect a requirement to a mechanism and its trade-off
mcqs.explanation: A justified design choice explains why it serves this problem.

mcqs.q: What does a screenshot of a login screen establish?
options: That all users can access the system
mcqs.explanation: Evidence supports limited claims; interface appearance does not prove security behaviour.

mcqs.q: Which performance statement is most assessable?
options: p95 was 240 ms at 100 requests/s in the stated test environment
mcqs.explanation: A metric, workload and environment let the audience interpret the result.

mcqs.q: Which structure provides a coherent technical narrative?
mcqs.explanation: A narrative should explain the reasoning and supporting observations.

mcqs.q: What should a diagram legend explain?
mcqs.explanation: Explicit notation prevents viewers guessing the intended relationships.

mcqs.q: Which visual choice improves accessibility?
options: Combine colour with labels or symbols
Distinguish states only by red and green
mcqs.explanation: Multiple visual cues preserve meaning when colours are hard to distinguish.

mcqs.q: What should accompany a benchmark chart?
options: Units, workload, environment and measurement context
mcqs.explanation: Measurement context is needed to assess relevance and limits.

mcqs.q: Why prepare an appendix?
options: Keep supporting detail available without interrupting the main narrative
mcqs.explanation: Appendices support follow-up questions while keeping the main talk focused.

mcqs.q: What is the purpose of a demo script?
options: Define starting state, actions and expected outcomes
mcqs.explanation: A repeatable journey makes the demonstration purposeful and easier to rehearse.

mcqs.q: The live demo fails and time is short. What is the best response?
options: Acknowledge it, try a bounded recovery, then use a labelled fallback
mcqs.explanation: Honest fallback handling preserves time and the distinction between evidence types.

mcqs.q: What is a meaningful negative demo case?
options: Hiding the error message from the audience
Showing that an unauthorised action is rejected
mcqs.explanation: A rejected misuse case can demonstrate a specific guard under the tested conditions.

mcqs.q: Why rehearse aloud with the actual setup?
options: Speaking, transitions and demo steps all consume time
Silent reading always predicts delivery time
mcqs.explanation: Full rehearsal exposes timing and environment problems that slide review misses.

mcqs.q: When running late, what should be cut first?
options: The problem statement in every case
Optional detail while preserving the core claim and evidence
mcqs.explanation: Prioritised content allows a coherent shorter presentation.

mcqs.q: Which behaviour best supports team handoffs?
options: Rehearse clear transitions with consistent terminology
Let everyone repeat the full introduction
mcqs.explanation: Coordination reduces repetition and disruption.

mcqs.q: How should a speaker answer an ambiguous question?
options: Clarify the intended meaning before giving a specific answer
mcqs.explanation: A brief clarification helps address the actual concern.

mcqs.q: What is the best response to an unmeasured regional-failover question?
options: State it has not been tested and explain how it would be measured
Present a unit test as failover evidence
mcqs.explanation: Honest uncertainty preserves the boundary between measured results and assumptions.

mcqs.q: Why distinguish implemented from planned features?
options: Planned features count as completed tests
The audience needs an accurate account of the system's state
mcqs.explanation: Misrepresenting future work can lead to incorrect evaluation or decisions.

mcqs.q: Which code excerpt belongs on a slide?
options: A short section that supports the design point being explained
mcqs.explanation: Select code for explanatory value, not sheer volume.

mcqs.q: What should the final slide communicate?
options: The central result, limitation and requested next action
mcqs.explanation: The ending should help the audience retain the conclusion and know what follows.

techQuestions.q: Outline a ten-minute presentation for a student software project.
techQuestions.answer: Allocate roughly two minutes to the problem and requirements, two to design, three to a key workflow, two to quality evidence and limitations, and one to the conclusion. Adapt this to the actual rubric. Write a clear takeaway for each part and rehearse transitions. Keep detailed implementation material in an appendix so the main argument fits the time.

techQuestions.q: Explain the same queue design to a client and to an engineer.
techQuestions.answer: Tell the client that an order can remain safely pending while payment processing recovers, and explain the user-visible status. Tell the engineer about durability, consumer retries, idempotency, backlog limits and operational evidence. Both explanations must describe the same behaviour. Change the depth and vocabulary while retaining the trade-off that accepted work may complete later.

techQuestions.q: Turn “our app is fast” into a defensible presentation claim.
techQuestions.answer: Specify the user operation, workload, environment, duration and latency statistic, then report the measured value and error rate. For example, distinguish p95 response time at a given request rate from a single local request. Show the result with units and state the limits of extrapolation. Include resource or bottleneck observations if they explain the result.

techQuestions.q: Plan a live demonstration of access control.
techQuestions.answer: Prepare two sample accounts with different permissions and a known record. Show the permitted action, then attempt a relevant forbidden action through the interface or direct request. State the expected rejection and verify no protected content is returned. Avoid projecting credentials. Explain that this demonstrates selected cases and is supported by broader tests, not exhaustive proof of security.

techQuestions.q: What should happen when a demo's external service becomes unavailable?
techQuestions.answer: Briefly acknowledge the observed problem and attempt only the recovery rehearsed within the time budget. If that fails, switch to a clearly identified recording or screenshots and explain what they show. Distinguish the current failure from prior successful evidence. Continue the presentation and record a follow-up investigation rather than consuming all remaining time with debugging.

Decide which relationship the audience must understand, then remove unrelated details or split the view. Use readable labels, a legend, explicit boundaries and meaningful arrows. Introduce the whole system briefly, highlight the relevant path and explain its consequence. Put the full diagram in an appendix. Preserve necessary evidence rather than shrinking every label to fit more boxes.

techQuestions.q: How can a chart mislead even when its numbers are correct?
techQuestions.answer: An unexplained truncated axis can exaggerate differences, averages can conceal slow-tail behaviour, and unmatched workloads can make comparisons unfair. Missing units or environments further obscure interpretation. State the measurement method and use an appropriate scale. Explain any necessary axis truncation and show the statistics relevant to the claim rather than selecting only flattering values.

techQuestions.q: Design a useful rehearsal feedback process.
techQuestions.answer: Run the talk aloud with the actual slides and demo, time each section and ask a listener to restate the central claim. Note where explanations, terminology or visuals caused confusion. Record unsupported claims and fragile transitions. Revise those areas, then repeat the affected parts. A rehearsal should produce specific changes, not merely familiarity with the script.

techQuestions.q: How should a team distribute speaking roles?
techQuestions.answer: Assign coherent sections with explicit handoff sentences and a shared vocabulary. Rehearse the control and device transitions and check for duplicated explanations. Each member should understand the problem, overall design and key limitations so questions can be routed appropriately. Balance participation within the presentation's purpose rather than splitting content into disconnected equal-sized fragments.

techQuestions.q: An examiner challenges your claim that the system scales. How should you respond?
techQuestions.answer: Answer with the precise evidence you have: tested load range, environment, latency, throughput, errors and bottlenecks. Explain whether capacity was actually increased and measured. If you only ran a small demonstration, narrow the claim and describe the next capacity experiment. Do not replace missing measurements with architectural labels such as microservices or cloud.

techQuestions.q: How do you present unfinished work honestly without losing the narrative?
techQuestions.answer: Separate completed and verified behaviour from planned work. Explain the practical impact of the limitation, what remains usable, and the next task or decision needed. Tie it back to the requirement rather than giving a vague disclaimer. A clear account of scope and evidence helps the audience evaluate the current result and judge the proposed next step.

techQuestions.q: Build a claim-evidence-limitation chain for reliable order processing.
techQuestions.answer: Claim that pending orders survive a bounded worker outage. Show the queue and worker design, then demonstrate stopping a worker, submitting work, restarting and observing completion. Support it with queue and order identifiers and duplicate-effect checks. State limits such as queue retention and outage duration. Propose longer outage and failure-injection tests before claiming broader resilience.

flashcards.definition: Identifying listeners' knowledge, concerns and decisions before selecting content.
What the audience should understand or decide by the end.
A connected explanation of problem, constraints, approach, evidence and consequences.
A statement about the system that needs suitable supporting evidence.
Observations or artifacts that support a specific, bounded claim.
A boundary on what was implemented, measured or established.
A repeatable starting state, action sequence and expected outcome.
Clearly labelled alternative material used when a live demonstration cannot proceed.
Explicitly guiding the audience through transitions and relationships.
Supporting detail available for questions without interrupting the main story.
Information conveyed through readable, distinguishable cues rather than colour alone.
Practising complete delivery to find timing, clarity and setup problems.
